active_themes.label: Confirmation Backdrop Unchanged
active_themes.summary: No direct news on Warsh confirmation today, but the geopolitical relief (Iran deal signal) reduces the acute pressure on Powell's May timeline. Warsh confirmation remains on track procedurally. The underlying issue persists: markets are watching whether the Fed will make policy decisions under political duress rather than data independence.

active_themes.label: Iran Deal Hopes Surface
active_themes.summary: Today's headlines show Iran signaling willingness to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, following the ceasefire extension precedent. Oil dropped sharply and the dollar weakened—textbook risk-off-to-risk-on reversal. This validates the market's 3-week assumption that escalation risk is real but not yet inevitable. The test remains unchanged: whether the next escalation (vessel seizure, drone strike, or blockade attempt) breaks the negotiation framework and reprices to sustained disruption.

active_themes.label: Decisions Made Under Threat
active_themes.summary: The pattern has a new data point: Apple cut its high-yield savings account rate by 15 basis points, joining the collapse of federal Grad PLUS loan access. These are not isolated moves—they are the observable output of lenders de-risking at the institutional level. When every major financial institution moves in the same direction simultaneously (reducing consumer credit exposure), it signals fear of downstream default risk. That fear is being driven by energy-shock inflation expectations, not by actual employment weakness yet.

active_themes.label: Lender De-risking Accelerates
active_themes.summary: Apple's 15bp savings rate cut is the second major data point (after federal student loan collapse) confirming lenders are retreating before a consumer shock hits. This is not panic—it is rational de-risking. Institutions see energy-shock inflation expectations and are lowering consumer credit exposure in advance. The setup is complete: if employment stays strong and inflation drops, credit tightening is a non-event; if either weakens, the reduced credit availability becomes a multiplier on consumer spending weakness.
